title: Prologue to Nemesinus: seven dialogues on the consubstantial Trinity
english: Things about God are hard to reach even for those well trained and ready to gaze into mysteries, and to see what lies beyond every mind [[in a mirror and in a riddle >> Bible:1Corinthians 13:12]], as the wisest Paul says. Human speech is thick, and cannot keep step with how thin our thoughts are. So there is much fear in speaking about God, and it is wise to choose silence here — yet not without cost for those charged to teach. Knowing this, the divine Paul said, [[Woe to me if I do not proclaim the gospel >> Bible:1Corinthians 9:16]].

I have therefore come to write the present book, and again for you, most studious brother Nemesinus, I have worked out the discourse on the holy and consubstantial Trinity. Gathering the thoughts on each question as by kind or form, we composed the whole body of the book in seven short discourses; and because Hermias is most fond of letters and often asks about such things, we have addressed them to that most gentle man.

The style is relaxed, and the talk proceeds as question and answer through two speakers. The letter α is set before the first, β before the second. Because what is sought is very subtle, so that by questions and answers the matter under test may always be built up and torn down keenly, bringing in the speakers became necessary. Guard carefully the letters set before them. That way we will keep the finding of thoughts unconfused and set in the best order, and the arrangement and force of the whole book. I pray you be well in the Lord, beloved.

title: Dialogue 1 opening: Hermias after the storm; Be still and know
english: A. Yesterday and the day before we could not see sacred Hermias — he seemed neither to shop, I think, nor to go out, but the storm kept him home; that is likely enough. Now fair weather has barely shown bright.
B. You speak the truth. Old age is always hard to please, and most reluctant to go outside when it rains hardest.

A. Then it is graceful and straight speech, if someone chooses, to compare you to the fish in the sea: when a harsh and ill-sounding wind churns the surge and leaps down roaring, they slip one by one and in schools into the hollows in the deep, and diving into the blooming weed as into a wood or thicket, they invent what helps them; but when the gleam of the sun’s ray swims upon the waters and they look out on the whole sea as if already smiling, they take heart, swim up again, and frolic on the crests of the waves, sending fear and hesitation away together.
B. Know well that my case is no other than that, my friend.
A. And for now you are far from crowd and business, and your mind is at rest by the hearth, as I suppose.
B. And what follows from that?
A. Very great and holy-seeming benefit. Or shall we not grant quiet some share among good things?
A. For what is sung from God through the Psalmist’s lyre will surely show the word about this to be true.

A. [[Be still and know that I am God >> Bible:Psalm 46:10]]. Bodily sight, free of dust and smoke and everything that can cloud it, sends a fine and unhindered energy upon the things that usually fall under it. But if some passion wounds it, it strikes the things seen less than it should, and will sometimes miss exactness itself — and that is no surprise. The human mind, if it is quiet and settled and used to leaving stale and foul imagination, will look sharp and clear and take in unerring knowledge of what is. But if some passion thickens it, it will never see through to the divine beauty itself, and will settle as on denser things — like birds soaked through, robbed of upward flight by being bound.
